title: The Bronzes of Benin, 1897–1899
subtitle: The Phillips mission, the punitive expedition, the taking of the palace's brasses and ivories, the Oba's trial and exile, and the objects' sale and reception in Europe, 1896–1903 (with a coda to 2022)
intro: In January 1897 the Kingdom of Benin, in what is now southern Nigeria, was observing Igue, the festival of the king's renewal, during which the Oba could receive no strangers. The British acting Consul-General of the Niger Coast Protectorate, James Phillips, set out to visit the Oba anyway. He wanted to open trade on the rivers and had asked London's leave to depose the king. The Oba's messengers asked him to wait. On 4 January, on the forest road from Gwato, Benin soldiers attacked the party; Phillips and most of his officers were killed with many of their carriers, and two officers escaped.

Within five weeks a naval force under Rear-Admiral Rawson had landed. It took Benin City on 18 February 1897, and three days later fire destroyed much of the city and the palace. From the palace the force removed thousands of objects: several hundred cast brass plaques that had lined its pillars, commemorative heads of past kings with carved tusks set into them, ivories, coral regalia and wooden figures. The officers' accounts described the city through its sacrifices and called it the City of Blood. Those descriptions were offered as the justification for the conquest; how accurate they were, and how far they reflected emergency rites in a city under attack, is still argued.

This chapter follows the objects from the palace to the sale room and the museum, and the king from the forest to the court and into exile. The record is uneven. On the British side there are a surgeon's diary, a survivor's book, despatches, a sailor's letter and the museum and dealers' registers. No writing by Oba Ovonramwen survives. His words reach us through messages reported by British officers and through the British court record of his trial. The Edo account was written down a generation later by Jacob Egharevba from the palace's own tradition. The chapter sets these out as positions and marks the later testimony as later.

The surprise in Europe was real and revealing. Curators trained on Renaissance metalwork found casting they compared to Cellini's, and at first credited it to Portuguese teachers; within a few years Luschan in Berlin and Ling Roth in Halifax were arguing that it was African. Webster's priced catalogues show how quickly the works became stock. The sale funded the expedition's costs and scattered the palace's collection across museums in Britain, Germany and the United States. A short coda notes the returns that began in the 2020s, as positions rather than a verdict.

Violence here is reported soberly. The killings of January and February are given in outline, and the expedition's claims about human sacrifice are reported as claims, without their detail. The record is mostly letters, logs, despatches, catalogues and published accounts rather than private diaries, and each eye is tagged accordingly.
calendar_note: All dates are in the Gregorian calendar. The Edo ritual year places Igue, the king's festival of renewal, around the turn of December and January; British sources call it the 'custom' for the king's father or the Ague festival. Some dates differ between sources: Phillips's sailing from Old Calabar is given as 17 or 27 December 1896, Rawson's appointment as 12 or 13 January 1897, and the Oba's deportation as 13 or 15 September 1897. Where only the year of a sale or publication is known, entries are dated to the year.

eyes.name: Ovonramwen Nogbaisi, Oba of Benin
eyes.role: Oba (king) of Benin, about forty in 1897; ritual and political head of the Edo kingdom, whose palace held the brass plaques, commemorative heads and carved tusks
eyes.where: Benin City; in the forest after February 1897; Calabar in exile from September 1897
eyes.vantage_label: the king whose palace was taken
eyes.form: recorded statements (messages reported by British officers; his defence as summarised in the 1897 trial record printed by Ling Roth, 1903)
eyes.authenticity: No writing by Ovonramwen himself survives. His messages to Phillips are known from Boisragon's 1897 account, and his defence at the September 1897 trial is known from the British court record as summarised and printed in Ling Roth's Great Benin (1903). Both were recorded by the side that tried him, through interpreters. Edo oral and court tradition, first written down by Egharevba (1933–34), gives the palace's view.
eyes.bio: Ovonramwen became Oba in 1888. British officials and traders accused him of blocking trade on the rivers, and the 1892 Gallwey treaty was read differently in Benin and in Old Calabar. His recorded position was that he had asked the British visitors to wait until the festival was over and had not ordered their deaths. He was deposed, tried by the Consul-General and exiled to Calabar, where he died in 1914.

sources.title: Ling Roth, Great Benin (Halifax, 1903), trial record in Section III — Utrecht University digitised copy
Igbafe, 'The Fall of Benin: A Reassessment', Journal of African History (1970)

eyes.name: James Robert Phillips
eyes.role: Acting Consul-General of the Niger Coast Protectorate, aged 33
eyes.where: Old Calabar; then up the Benin River to Gwato and the road to Benin City
eyes.vantage_label: the official who set out for Benin City
eyes.authenticity: His despatches of 16–17 November 1896 are in the Foreign Office papers at The National Archives, Kew (FO 2 series), and are catalogued by Digital Benin. The wording usually quoted from them comes from secondary works and has not been checked here against the originals.
eyes.bio: Phillips had been appointed to the Protectorate in 1896 and was acting for the Consul-General, Ralph Moor, who was on leave. He asked London for permission to go to Benin City and depose the Oba if necessary, and set out before a reply came. He and most of his party were killed on the road on 4 January 1897.

sources.title: Wikipedia: James Robert Phillips (summary of the despatches)
Digital Benin: FO 2/120 correspondence file

eyes.name: Alan Maxwell Boisragon
eyes.role: Captain, commandant of the Niger Coast Protectorate Force, aged 36; one of two European survivors of the Phillips party
eyes.where: With the Phillips party on the Gwato road; five days in the forest; back at the coast; home to England 16 March 1897
eyes.authenticity: The Benin Massacre (London: Methuen, 1897), written, he says, about two months after he reached England. It is a dated, day-by-day narrative but was composed after the punitive expedition and argues its case. An online transcription is at cristoraul.org.
eyes.bio: Boisragon commanded the Protectorate's armed constabulary but went with Phillips unarmed, at Phillips's insistence that the visit be peaceful. He and the district commissioner Ralph Locke, both wounded, hid in the forest for five days before reaching the creek. His book is the main English source for the Oba's messages asking for delay and for the march itself.

sources.title: Boisragon, The Benin Massacre (1897), online transcription

eyes.name: Felix Norman Roth
eyes.role: Medical officer with the Niger Coast Protectorate forces, attached to the advance column
eyes.where: Ceri and Ologbo camps; the march to Benin City; inside the city 18–22 February 1897
eyes.authenticity: 'A Diary of a Surgeon with the Benin Punitive Expedition', first printed in the Journal of the Manchester Geographical Society and reprinted as Appendix II of his brother Henry Ling Roth's Great Benin (1903). The 1903 index misprints his initials as 'E. N.'. Daily entries survive from 6 to about 22 February 1897 in the reprint.
eyes.bio: Roth was a doctor, not a fighting officer, and his diary is about water, heat, wounds, sanitation and camp life as much as about battle. He spoke with the survivors Locke and Boisragon in camp, treated the wounded on the march, and described the palace's brass heads and tusks the day after the city fell. Three days later he watched the fire that destroyed much of the city and his own medical stores.

sources.title: Ling Roth, Great Benin (1903), Appendix II — Utrecht digitised copy
UNE: 'The making of Great Benin: Felix Norman Roth and Henry Ling Roth'

eyes.name: Sir Harry Holdsworth Rawson
eyes.role: Rear-Admiral, Commander-in-Chief Cape of Good Hope and West Coast of Africa station; commander of the punitive expedition
eyes.where: Flagship off the Brass River; the march to Benin City; back at the Cape by May 1897
eyes.authenticity: His despatch of 27 February 1897 to the Admiralty is cited in the Admiralty's reply of 5 May 1897, printed in the London Gazette of 7 May 1897. Its full text has not been consulted here.
eyes.bio: Rawson was given command on 12 January 1897, a week after news of the killings reached London. He assembled a naval brigade of about 1,200 sailors and marines with Protectorate troops and thousands of carriers. His despatch is the official naval account of the campaign.

sources.title: London Gazette, 7 May 1897, issue 26850, p. 2534 (Admiralty letter to Rawson)

eyes.name: Reginald Hugh Spencer Bacon
eyes.role: Commander RN, intelligence officer of the expedition, aged 33
eyes.where: Reconnaissance on the creeks; the march to Benin City
eyes.authenticity: Benin: The City of Blood (London: Edward Arnold, 1897). Written up shortly after the campaign from his notes. The title is the expedition's own framing of the city and was widely repeated in the British press.
eyes.bio: Bacon later became an admiral and a pioneer of British submarines. In 1897 he scouted the Ologbo creek with Gallwey before the column crossed and kept the expedition's intelligence record. His book gave the campaign its popular name in Britain and set out the justification its officers offered: that the city was a place of sacrifice that had to be ended.

sources.title: Ling Roth, Great Benin (1903), Appendix II (Roth's diary mentions Bacon, 8 Feb 1897)

eyes.name: Herbert Sutherland Walker
eyes.role: Captain, attached to the Niger Coast Protectorate Force for the expedition; later Lieutenant-Colonel
eyes.where: With the Protectorate troops on the march and in Benin City
eyes.vantage_label: officer on the march, keeping a private diary
eyes.authenticity: A private diary kept by the family. Not published in full; passages have been quoted in recent studies, and in 2014 his grandson gave a copy to the Oba of Benin. Individual dated entries have not been consulted here.
eyes.bio: Walker is named, with Captain O'Shee, in Lieutenant-Colonel Hamilton's report of commendations printed in the London Gazette in May 1897. He kept two brass objects from the palace, a bird and a bell. His grandson, who inherited them, has said that the diary shows Walker's respect for the people of Benin and calls the objects loot.

sources.title: Modern Ghana: 'Walker and the restitution of two Benin bronzes' (2014)
London Gazette, 7 May 1897, p. 2534 (Hamilton's commendation)

eyes.name: Edward Higgins
eyes.role: Able seaman, HMS Theseus, in the naval brigade
eyes.where: On the march and in Benin City
eyes.form: dated letters (to his parents, printed in the press)
eyes.authenticity: A letter home to his parents in Hartlepool, printed in British newspapers and reprinted in the Manawatu Herald (New Zealand), 17 June 1897. The letter's own date is not given in the reprint.
eyes.bio: Higgins is one of very few ordinary sailors whose words about the campaign reached print. He wrote about thirst, fever and two dead marines, and he repeated the descriptions of sacrifice that the officers' accounts also gave. His letter shows how the 'city of blood' framing travelled from the column into family letters and onward to newspapers around the empire.

sources.title: Manawatu Herald, 17 June 1897, p. 2, 'A City of Blood' (Papers Past)

eyes.name: Sir Ralph Denham Rayment Moor
eyes.role: Consul-General and Commissioner of the Niger Coast Protectorate
eyes.where: On leave in England in January 1897; with the expedition in February; Benin City for the trial in September
eyes.vantage_label: the civil authority who tried the Oba
eyes.authenticity: His covering despatch, with Lieutenant-Colonel Hamilton's report from Benin City dated 23 February 1897, was printed in the London Gazette of 7 May 1897. The trial record of September 1897 is known chiefly through the summary printed in Ling Roth's Great Benin (1903).
eyes.bio: Moor was Phillips's superior and was on leave when Phillips set out. He returned with the punitive expedition, sent the palace plaques to the Foreign Office, and in September 1897 opened the court that tried the Oba and the chiefs. Igbafe and later historians note that he acted as both prosecutor and judge.

sources.title: London Gazette, 7 May 1897, issue 26850, pp. 2531–2534
Ling Roth, Great Benin (1903), Section III

eyes.name: Charles Hercules Read (with Ormonde Maddock Dalton)
eyes.role: Keeper of British and Medieval Antiquities and Ethnography at the British Museum (Read), and his senior assistant (Dalton)
eyes.vantage_label: curators in London receiving the plaques
eyes.authenticity: The museum's registers and correspondence (Af1898,0115 series) and their folio Antiquities from the City of Benin and from Other Parts of West Africa in the British Museum (London, 1899; 61 pp., 32 plates). The Digital Benin project now publishes the registers with curators' commentary.
eyes.bio: Read and Dalton were specialists in medieval and Renaissance European objects, which shaped how they looked at the plaques. They praised the casting as equal to the best European work and, like most writers of the time, credited Portuguese contact for it. Their 1899 folio, with photographs of the plates, became the standard reference for the dispersed objects.

sources.title: Digital Benin: BM plaque Af1898,0115.93 with curator's history of the 1897 loan and display
Read & Dalton 1899, bibliographic description

eyes.name: Felix von Luschan
eyes.role: Director's assistant (later Director) of the African and Oceanian department, Königliches Museum für Völkerkunde, Berlin
eyes.where: Berlin; at the London sales in summer 1897
eyes.form: dated letters, telegrams and published studies
eyes.authenticity: His letters and acquisition files are in the Ethnologisches Museum archive (files on 'Erwerbung ethnologischer Gegenstände aus der Benin-Expedition', catalogued on Proveana). His three-volume Die Altertümer von Benin appeared in 1919. Details of his 1897 buying here come from a 2022 Spektrum article drawing on that archive.
eyes.bio: Luschan, born in Austria and trained in Vienna, made Berlin the largest single buyer of Benin objects outside Britain, assembling more than 580 of them. He argued in print that the works were African art of the highest order, not the product of European teachers. He also held to 'rescue' collecting and supported German colonial rule.

sources.title: Spektrum.de: 'Felix von Luschan – Jäger der geraubten Beninbronzen' (2022)
Staatliche Museen zu Berlin: The Benin Collection in Berlin

eyes.name: William Downing Webster
eyes.side: London and provincial art and curio trade
eyes.authenticity: Webster's Illustrated Catalogue of Ethnological Specimens appeared in numbered parts from the late 1890s to about 1901, with photographic plates and stock numbers. Stock numbers painted on objects allow museums to trace them to his catalogues.
eyes.bio: Webster became the leading dealer in Benin material after 1897, buying from officers and at auction and selling to Pitt-Rivers, to Berlin, to university museums and to collectors. His catalogues priced plaques and heads individually. They are now key evidence for where the palace objects went.

sources.title: MAA Cambridge, plaque E 1900.98.1 (Webster catalogue vol. 3 no. 21, 1899)

eyes.name: Henry Ling Roth
eyes.role: Anthropologist and museum curator in Halifax, Yorkshire; brother of the surgeon Felix Roth
eyes.authenticity: Great Benin: Its Customs, Art and Horrors (Halifax: F. King & Sons, 1903; 275 illustrations; 320 copies for sale). It gathers travellers' accounts from the 1500s onward, the trial record of 1897 and his brother's diary. Digitised by Utrecht University Library.
eyes.bio: Ling Roth never went to Benin. His book set the art beside the 'horrors' of its subtitle, which repeats the expedition's framing, but it also collected the earlier European descriptions of a large, ordered city and gave careful attention to the casting. It remains a basic source and a document of how Britain explained 1897 to itself.

sources.title: Great Benin (1903), Utrecht University digitised copy

eyes.name: Jacob Uwadiae Egharevba
eyes.role: Edo historian, later a chief and first curator of the Benin museum (1946); a child in Benin territory in 1897
eyes.vantage_label: Edo court historian, writing a generation later
eyes.form: chronicle (written later, from palace and oral tradition)
eyes.authenticity: Ekhere vb Itan Edo (Lagos: CMS Press, 1933) and A Short History of Benin (Lagos, 1934; revised 1953, 1960, 1968). Built from interviews with palace officials, priests and elders under Obas Eweka II and Akenzua II. Written decades after 1897, so it is listed here as later testimony, not as an eyewitness record.
eyes.bio: Egharevba was about four in 1897. Working with the permission of Ovonramwen's son and grandson, he wrote the first history of Benin by an Edo author, recording the palace's account of the festival, the visit and the exile. His books are the chief written channel for the Edo oral tradition about 1897.

sources.title: National Museums Liverpool: 'Chief Egharevba, a pioneer historian of Benin'

entries.headline: Phillips asks London for leave to go to Benin City
entries.digest: Phillips wrote to the Foreign Office that the Oba was blocking trade and that the Protectorate would have to act. He asked permission to visit Benin City early in the new year, with an armed force in reserve if the Oba would not receive him, and proposed deposing the Oba. The despatch went on 17 November. The reply, when it came, was cautious, but he had already left.
entries.source_note: Despatch no. 105 of 16 Nov 1896 and its forwarding on 17 Nov, as summarised in the Wikipedia articles on Phillips and the 1897 expedition; original in FO 2 series, Kew, not checked.

entries.headline: The Oba asks the visitors to wait
entries.digest: Word came to Benin that the acting Consul-General intended to visit. According to Boisragon, the Oba's reply was that he was performing the rites for his late father, the annual festival during which the king could receive no strangers, and asked that the visit be put off for one or two months. Boisragon also records the request that the Consul-General come with only one Itsekiri chief and no other white men. In Edo tradition the festival is Igue, the most sacred season of the royal year.
entries.source_note: Boisragon, The Benin Massacre (1897), ch. on the King's messages; Edo tradition per Egharevba (1934). Exact day of the message not established.

entries.place: Old Calabar, aboard the yacht Ivy
entries.headline: Phillips's party sails from Old Calabar
entries.digest: Boisragon dates the departure from Old Calabar aboard the Protectorate yacht Ivy to 27 December. The party went round by sea and up the Benin River. Phillips insisted that the officers carry no arms in sight and that the visit be presented as peaceful. Other accounts give 17 December for this sailing.
entries.source_note: Boisragon (1897) as transcribed at cristoraul.org; Wikipedia's Phillips article gives 17 Dec.

entries.headline: 'The City of Blood' is published
entries.digest: Bacon's book, published by Edward Arnold, told the campaign from the intelligence officer's notes. Its title gave the British public a two-word case for the expedition, and later writers on both sides have quoted it ever since: as justification, or as evidence of how the conquest was framed.
entries.source_note: Bibliographic record; month of publication not established.

entries.headline: Messengers at Gwato ask for two days
entries.digest: When the party reached Gwato, the Oba's messengers asked Phillips to wait two days so that the king could prepare to receive them. Phillips refused and kept to his timetable. Boisragon later read the messages as cover for an ambush. The Edo account, recorded by Egharevba a generation later, holds that the Oba wished the visit to wait and that the attack was the decision of war chiefs, not the king.
entries.source_note: Boisragon (1897), at Gwato on 3 Jan; Edo view per Egharevba (1934) and Igbafe (1970).

entries.headline: The party is attacked on the road
entries.digest: Phillips led the party out of Gwato in the morning along the narrow forest road towards Benin City. In the afternoon, near the village of Ugbine, Benin soldiers under the war chief Ologbosere attacked the column. Phillips and most of the British officers were killed, with an unknown number of the African carriers; many Itsekiri carriers were taken captive. The size of the African loss was never established.
entries.source_note: Wikipedia summaries of the expedition and of Phillips; Boisragon (1897); trial verdict printed in Ling Roth (1903) names 4 Jan.

entries.headline: Boisragon and Locke escape into the forest
entries.digest: Boisragon and Locke, both wounded, got off the path into the bush that afternoon. He calls it the worst day and night he ever spent. They had no food and moved mostly by night, trying to find the creek.
entries.quote: the most awful day and night I have ever passed
entries.source_note: Boisragon (1897), chapter on the attack.

entries.headline: Five days in the bush, then a canoe
entries.digest: After a last night in the bush on Friday the 8th, the two men reached water at dawn, then a village where people fed them and took them down the creek by canoe. At dusk they met a Protectorate launch and were carried to New Benin that night. Boisragon calls it a resurrection.
entries.quote: a veritable resurrection from the dead
entries.source_note: Boisragon (1897).

entries.headline: Rawson is given command
entries.digest: With news of the killings in London within the week, the Foreign Office and the Admiralty agreed on a punitive expedition. Rear-Admiral Rawson, commanding the Cape and West Africa station, was appointed to lead it. Ships and marines were gathered from the Cape, the Mediterranean and home waters.
entries.source_note: Wikipedia (12 Jan); Smarthistory gives 13 Jan.

entries.headline: A captain's diary names the loot
entries.digest: Walker's private diary covered the expedition. According to his grandson, at least three entries refer to objects being taken as loot, and Walker himself kept two brass pieces from the palace, a bird and a bell. The diary has not been published in full, and the dated entries have not been seen here.
entries.source_note: Modern Ghana, June 2014, reporting Mark Walker's account of the diary.

entries.headline: The Oba leaves his city
entries.digest: Ovonramwen and his household left the city before the British entered and spent about six months moving through the country beyond their reach. The British offered terms for his surrender and searched for him. Chiefs were tried and some executed in the months that followed.
entries.source_note: Wikipedia (IPFS mirror) on Ovonramwen; Ling Roth (1903) Section III.

entries.headline: Roth's diary opens at Ceri
entries.digest: The column reached Ceri at four in the afternoon and the advance party camped in the village. Roth's first concern as medical officer was water and sanitation for the naval column that was coming in behind.
entries.source_note: F. N. Roth, diary, in Ling Roth, Great Benin (1903), Appendix II.

entries.headline: Bacon scouts the creek
entries.digest: Roth notes that Gallwey and Bacon went up the Ologbo creek by canoe to scout the crossing. Bacon's book later set out the route and the problems of the swamp. Roth spent the day finding and damming a spring for the camp.
entries.source_note: Roth diary, 8 Feb 1897, in Ling Roth (1903).

entries.headline: The surgeon talks with the two survivors
entries.digest: Roth sat with Locke and Boisragon, who had come up with the force, and heard their account of 4 January. Plans were made for bridging the Ologbo creek and the column's duties were laid out. The next day the bridge was judged impossible and Boisragon was sent home sick.
entries.source_note: Roth diary, 10–11 Feb 1897, in Ling Roth (1903).

entries.headline: The column crosses at Ologbo
entries.digest: Because the swamp made bridging impossible, the troops went up the creek by launch and boat. The village of Ologbo was shelled and taken, and an officer was wounded. Roth set up his first dressing station.
entries.source_note: Roth diary, 12 Feb; matching account in the despatch printed in the London Gazette, 7 May 1897, p. 2531.

entries.headline: The admiral crosses, unwell in the heat
entries.digest: Rawson and his headquarters staff crossed to Ologbo. Roth noted that the admiral was suffering from the heat and that the naval columns had taken losses at Gwato and Sapoba, where diversionary forces had gone in.
entries.source_note: Gazette despatch p. 2531 (13 Feb); Roth diary, 13 Feb 1897.

entries.headline: An alarm before dawn and a field hospital
entries.digest: A false alarm before dawn was followed by a day of fighting along the path. Roth built a rough hospital for the wounded at the cross-roads camp. Water was already the column's chief worry.
entries.source_note: Roth diary, 15 Feb 1897.

entries.headline: A long running fight; six miles to go
entries.digest: After a day of skirmishing on the path, the column reached the abandoned village of Awoko. Roth reckoned it was about six miles from Benin City. Men were short of water and exhausted.
entries.source_note: Roth diary, 17 Feb 1897; Gazette p. 2531.

entries.headline: The city is taken in the afternoon
entries.digest: The despatch printed in the Gazette describes the last march from Awoko under constant fire and the entry into Benin City at about two in the afternoon, with exhausted men short of water. The Oba and his chiefs had left. The despatch presents the city through its sacrificial sites, the framing that the British accounts would repeat; how far those descriptions were accurate, and how far they reflected the emergency rites of a city under attack, is disputed.
entries.source_note: London Gazette, 7 May 1897, pp. 2531–2532.

entries.headline: The city falls, as Boisragon tells it
entries.digest: Boisragon, by then invalided home, wrote up the last day from fellow officers: about twenty-two miles of fighting along a narrow path, a square formed outside the city, a final charge and the palace occupied that night. A naval surgeon was among the dead. None of the hostages from his own party were found alive, but a few carriers were recovered.
entries.source_note: Boisragon (1897), final chapters.

entries.headline: Brass heads with tusks, embossed doors
entries.digest: The day after the city fell, Roth walked through the palace compound. He described brass heads standing in rows with carved tusks set into holes in their tops, figures he called beautiful idols, and doors covered with embossed brass showing figures. He mixed this with what he called the grim condition of the city, which he described at length, as did the other British accounts. Water and supply parties went out under fire.
entries.source_note: Roth diary, 19 Feb 1897, in Ling Roth (1903).

entries.headline: A sailor writes home about the city
entries.digest: Higgins wrote to his parents about the march, the thirst, the fever and the two marines who died. He repeated the reports of sacrifice that the whole column was being told and shown, and said he never wished to see such sights again. The letter was printed under the headline 'A City of Blood' as it went round the British and colonial press.
entries.source_note: Manawatu Herald, 17 June 1897, p. 2; the letter's own date is not given.

entries.headline: Fire sweeps the city
entries.digest: A fire, which Roth says was started by carriers and driven by wind, spread across the town, destroying much of it and most of the medical stores and the men's kit. He watched it go from roof to roof. When it was over he noted only that the air was cleaner.
entries.quote: the flames passing from house to house
entries.source_note: Roth diary, 21 Feb 1897.

entries.headline: Hamilton reports the palace burned
entries.digest: Lieutenant-Colonel Hamilton's report, dated Benin City 23 February and forwarded by Moor, records that fire on the 21st destroyed the king's quarters and all those around them. It also notes the altars where carved tusks stood in brass heads, some with a pair of brass cockerels. The effects of Phillips's party, found in the palaver house, were lost in the same fire.
entries.source_note: Hamilton to Moor, Benin City, 23 Feb 1897, London Gazette 7 May 1897, p. 2532.

entries.headline: The admiral leaves with the wounded
entries.digest: Rawson left Benin City with the naval brigade and the wounded on the 22nd. Roth praised his own servant, Charles Nartey, in that day's entry. The Protectorate troops stayed to hold the town until the chiefs submitted.
entries.source_note: Roth diary, 22 Feb 1897; Hamilton's report, Gazette p. 2532.

entries.headline: Rawson's despatch to the Admiralty
entries.digest: Rawson reported the operations to the Admiralty on 27 February, from the capture of the city on the 18th to the withdrawal. The Admiralty's reply of 5 May approved his measures, praised the speed with which the force was assembled, and listed the officers he commended.
entries.source_note: Admiralty to Rawson, 5 May 1897, London Gazette 7 May 1897, p. 2534.

entries.headline: Boisragon reaches home and starts writing
entries.digest: Boisragon landed in England on 16 March. About two months later he wrote the book that became The Benin Massacre, published by Methuen before the year was out. It was the survivor's account and carried the official case for the expedition.
entries.source_note: Boisragon (1897), author's note on writing two months after reaching home.

entries.headline: The despatches are published
entries.digest: The London Gazette printed the despatches, Hamilton's report and the Admiralty's letter to Rawson, with honours for the officers. For British readers this was the official account: a punitive expedition, a short campaign, and casualties that the despatch said could not be considered heavy.
entries.source_note: London Gazette, issue 26850, 7 May 1897, pp. 2531–2534.

entries.headline: The first sale of the spoils
entries.digest: Objects from the palace that fell to the naval officers were put up at Stevens's Auction Rooms in Covent Garden. The sale was organised on the Admiralty's behalf, and accounts say its purpose was to help meet the costs of the expedition. Other pieces stayed with officers or were sold through dealers.
entries.source_note: Wikipedia summary of the sale (date and venue); the purpose is as stated in the secondary literature, not checked against the sale catalogue.

entries.headline: The sailor's letter goes round the empire
entries.digest: Higgins's letter appeared in New Zealand under the headline 'A City of Blood', four months after the city fell. The same headline was Bacon's book title that year. A private letter had become part of the public justification.
entries.source_note: Manawatu Herald, 17 June 1897, p. 2.

entries.headline: Three hundred plaques arrive on loan
entries.digest: The Crown Agents, acting for the Foreign Office, lent the museum 304 brass plaques that Moor had sent home as the government's share of the spoils. Read and Dalton began to sort and study them. Each carried a Foreign Office number painted on it.
entries.source_note: British Museum curator's history in Digital Benin record Af1898,0115.93.

entries.headline: Luschan buys tusks in London
entries.digest: Luschan had heard that large quantities of carved ivory and bronze were coming onto the market and that tons of tusks were on their way to London. When he saw them he called the carved tusks museum masterpieces of the first rank. At two London auctions in August he bought 13 of the 50 tusks offered, borrowing 5,000 marks from his brother-in-law to do so.
entries.source_note: Spektrum.de (2022), from the Ethnologisches Museum archive.

entries.headline: Buy whatever can be had
entries.digest: From London Luschan telegraphed the German consul in Lagos, asking him to buy whatever Benin pieces were available regardless of price. The consul did, and thanked him later for the commission. Berlin thus bought both in London and directly in West Africa.
entries.source_note: Spektrum.de (2022); SMB Benin collection page names Consul Eduard Schmidt.

entries.headline: The Oba comes back to his city
entries.digest: After six months away, Ovonramwen came back into Benin City with seven or eight hundred unarmed followers, dressed in coral regalia. He offered the British oil and the location of buried ivory; the offer of ivory was refused because it had already been found. He was placed under guard.
entries.source_note: Ling Roth (1903), Section III; Wikipedia (IPFS mirror) on Ovonramwen.

entries.headline: He is told he is deposed
entries.digest: At the court house the acting Resident, Captain Roupell, called on him to submit. He made obeisance, and Roupell told him he was no longer king. The trial of the chiefs and of the Oba was set for Moor's return.
entries.source_note: Ling Roth (1903), Section III.

entries.headline: The plaques go on show
entries.digest: The plaques were hung in the Assyrian basement and opened to the public. They drew large crowds and press attention. For many visitors this was the first sight of cast metal of this quality from Africa, shown in the same rooms as the Assyrian palace reliefs.
entries.source_note: British Museum curator's history in Digital Benin record Af1898,0115.93.

entries.headline: Banishment for the Oba, death for chiefs
entries.digest: The court found six chiefs guilty of the massacre; two had died, one was passed over as a boy, two were sentenced to be shot, and Ologbosere, still at large, was condemned in his absence. Moor sentenced Ovonramwen to banishment and ordered him taken to Old Calabar.
entries.source_note: Ling Roth (1903), Section III. Exact day of sentence not established.

entries.headline: Moor opens the trial
entries.digest: The court sat at four in the afternoon, Moor presiding over a case in which he also stood for the government. Witnesses were heard on who ordered the attack of 4 January. The court adjourned to 3 September.
entries.source_note: Ling Roth (1903), Section III.

entries.headline: The Oba's defence: he never ordered the killings
entries.digest: As the court record summarises him, Ovonramwen said he had always been the white men's friend: he had exchanged presents with them and let Europeans visit his city. He said his orders had been that the white men were not to be killed, and that the attack was the work of the war chiefs. The court accepted that the chiefs had acted but held him responsible as king.
entries.quote: his orders were that the white men were not to be killed
entries.source_note: Ling Roth (1903), Section III, printing the 1897 court record (reported speech).

entries.place: Gwato, then by sea to Calabar
entries.headline: Taken to the yacht and into exile
entries.digest: Departure had been set for Monday 13 September. The record printed by Ling Roth says that on the 15th the king was brought down to Gwato in the early morning and put aboard the Protectorate yacht, restrained in a hammock. Two of his wives went with him to Calabar. Many accounts give 13 September as the date of deportation.
entries.source_note: Ling Roth (1903), Section III; wives named in Wikipedia (IPFS mirror).

entries.headline: Two hundred and three plaques become the nation's
entries.digest: The Foreign Office gave the museum 203 of the plaques, registered under the number Af1898,0115. In summer 1898 eleven more came; three were kept. The Foreign Office kept eight and offered the rest for sale to museums, collectors and dealers. Photographs of the unsold plaques were sent to prospective buyers.
entries.source_note: Digital Benin records Af1898,0115.93 and the 1897 photograph 5_51_1_1.

entries.headline: A plaque at five pounds
entries.digest: Among the plaques the Foreign Office sold, one showing a gong player went to Hans Meyer of Berlin for five pounds and was given to Luschan's museum the next year. Berlin went on to hold the largest Benin collection in Germany.
entries.source_note: Digital Benin record 5_51_1_1 (photograph of plaque with sale price).

entries.headline: A plaque priced in the catalogue
entries.digest: Part 21 of Webster's illustrated catalogue offered a plaque of a warrior, about twenty inches high, stock number 6244, at fifteen guineas. Cambridge's Museum of Archaeology and Anthropology bought it the next year. It is one of 116 Cambridge objects whose ownership passed to Nigeria in January 2026.
entries.source_note: MAA Cambridge record E 1900.98.1.

entries.headline: Read and Dalton's folio
entries.digest: Read and Dalton published Antiquities from the City of Benin, a large folio of 61 pages and 32 plates. They praised the casting as fit to stand with European Renaissance work, called its makers' society barbarous, and credited the Portuguese with teaching the craft. Later research has shown that the Benin casting tradition is far older than Portuguese contact.
entries.source_note: Bibliographic description; Smarthistory summary of their judgements.

entries.headline: Great Benin gathers the record
entries.digest: Ling Roth published Great Benin in a limited edition, with his brother's diary as an appendix and the trial record. His captions treat the plaques as evidence of local craft, noting where the native artist's hand shows in work others credited to Europeans. The subtitle, 'customs, art and horrors', keeps the expedition's frame.
entries.quote: the touch of the native artist makes itself visible
entries.source_note: Great Benin (1903), title page and caption to fig. 5.

entries.headline: The Oba dies in exile
entries.digest: Ovonramwen died in Calabar, still in exile, in January 1914. That year the British allowed his son to become Oba as Eweka II. His remains were later buried in the palace grounds in Benin City.
entries.source_note: Britannica; Wikipedia (IPFS mirror).

entries.headline: Three volumes on the antiquities of Benin
entries.digest: After about twenty years' work, Luschan published Die Altertümer von Benin in three volumes, trying to catalogue every known piece. He compared the best casting to Cellini's and argued that the art was African. It is still a reference work.
entries.source_note: SMB Benin collection page; Spektrum.de (2022); Smarthistory.

entries.headline: The first history by an Edo author
entries.digest: Egharevba published his history in Edo, drafted since 1921 from interviews at the palace and with elders. The next year he issued it in English as A Short History of Benin. Its account of 1897 is the palace's: the festival, the request to wait, the attack by chiefs, the exile. It was written more than thirty years after the event.
entries.source_note: National Museums Liverpool; Wikipedia, A Short History of Benin.

entries.headline: A grandson brings back a bird and a bell
entries.digest: On the centenary of Ovonramwen's death, Walker's grandson Mark Walker gave the Oba of Benin the brass bird and bell the captain had taken, with a copy of his grandfather's diary. The palace received him as a friend of the city.
entries.source_note: Modern Ghana, June 2014.

entries.headline: Germany hands back the first twenty
entries.digest: Germany's foreign minister handed over the first twenty bronzes in Abuja (Nigeria counted 22) after the two governments agreed earlier that year to transfer ownership of the Benin objects in German museums. Berlin signed over its 512 objects in August 2022; about a third stay on loan in Berlin. Positions differ: the German government called it a step in facing its colonial past; Nigeria's culture minister thanked Germany; the British Museum says the British Museum Act 1963 bars it from giving up its collection.
entries.source_note: NPR, 21 Dec 2022; SMB Benin collection page (25 Aug 2022). The British Museum's position is as widely reported.

claims.evidence: Hamilton's report, London Gazette 7 May 1897; Roth diary

convergences.label: Gwato: the request to wait
convergences.note: The same request for delay reads as courtesy and ritual necessity in the Edo account, as a stalling tactic to Boisragon after the fact, and as no reason to stop to Phillips.

convergences.label: The attack near Ugbine
convergences.note: Phillips did not survive to write; Boisragon wrote the survivor's book; the Oba's view is known only from his trial defence and from Edo tradition, which hold that the war chiefs acted without his order.

convergences.label: Ceri camp: the survivors and the surgeon
convergences.note: Roth hears the survivors' story in camp while Bacon scouts the creek; the expedition's account of the killings is being shaped as it marches.

convergences.label: The city taken
convergences.note: An official despatch, a survivor writing from others' reports, a surgeon's diary and a sailor's letter: four ranks, one framing of the city, and no Edo account written that day.

convergences.label: The fire
convergences.note: Roth blames carriers and watches his stores burn; Hamilton's report notes the palace's loss in a line; neither treats the destruction of the palace itself as a loss to anyone but the force.

convergences.label: London sales and the Oba's return
convergences.note: In the same weeks that Luschan bid for tusks in London and the plaques sat in the British Museum's stores, the king whose palace they came from walked back into his city and was told he was deposed.

convergences.label: Trial in Benin City, display in London
convergences.note: The Oba defended himself in a consular court as the plaques from his palace went on public view in Bloomsbury.

ties.note: Phillips sought to depose the Oba; the Oba asked him to wait until the festival was over.
Boisragon travelled in Phillips's party at his order, unarmed, and survived him.
Roth spoke with Boisragon and Locke in camp at Ceri on 10 February 1897.
Brothers: Henry Ling Roth reprinted Felix's diary as Appendix II of Great Benin.
Roth's diary records Bacon's canoe reconnaissance of the Ologbo creek on 8 February.
Moor presided at the trial and sentenced the Oba to banishment.
Phillips was acting for Moor while Moor was on leave; the expedition was mounted in Moor's jurisdiction.
Walker was commended in Hamilton's report, which Moor forwarded and the Gazette printed.
Both studied the same dispersed plaques; Luschan's catalogue built on the British Museum's photographs and Read and Dalton's folio, and both compared the casting to Renaissance work.
Berlin bought through the London trade in which Webster was the leading dealer.
Ling Roth printed the record of the Oba's trial, the main surviving summary of his defence.
Egharevba wrote the palace's history under Ovonramwen's son and grandson, giving the Edo account of 1897.
Higgins's letter and Bacon's book went out under the same phrase, 'city of blood'; the borrowing ran through the press, not between the two men.

threads_out.note: Paris in 1889 showed colonial pavilions and reconstructed African villages to millions of visitors. Eight years later London crowds queued to see Benin's plaques in the British Museum's Assyrian basement. Both were ways in which European publics saw Africa through the objects and people that empire had brought home.

Alain Locke's essay 'The Legacy of the Ancestral Arts' in The New Negro (1925) urged Black American artists to look to classic African sculpture. The Benin castings, scattered across European museums after 1897, were among the West African works that writers and artists of the Harlem Renaissance knew and admired.

Berlin's Benin collection, which Luschan built to more than 600 objects, lost dozens of pieces during the Second World War, leaving 512 historical objects. In 2022 ownership of those 512 passed to Nigeria.
